events.title: Christmas Day
events.text: Washington's army, 2,400 men and eighteen guns, marches from its camps around Newtown to McConkey's Ferry. Rall's brigade of three Hessian regiments holds Trenton nine miles downstream, with no works: Rall has refused to dig. Ewing is to cross below the town and Cadwalader at Bristol; the ice will stop them both.

events.title: The crossing
events.text: Glover's Marblehead fishermen begin ferrying the army in Durham boats and flat ferries at about six, ninety minutes after sunset, the river full of floating ice. The plan is to be over by midnight.

events.title: The storm
events.text: About eleven a nor'easter comes on: rain, then sleet and snow on a hard north-east wind. The last guns and horses are not over until three, three hours late. Washington gives up a dawn attack and goes on anyway.

events.title: The march on Trenton
events.text: At four the column moves off through the storm, up the bluff to the Bear Tavern and down through the ravine of Jacob's Creek, where the guns are lowered on ropes. Two men freeze to death on the road.

events.title: Birmingham
events.text: At the fork the army divides: Greene's division with Washington by the Pennington Road, Sullivan's by the River Road, each four and a half miles from the town. Sullivan reports his powder wet and is told to use the bayonet.

events.title: Eight o'clock
events.text: 'Exactly at eight' Greene's van drives in the Pennington Road picket; three minutes later Sullivan strikes the River Road. The jägers and the dragoons bolt over the Assunpink bridge. Forrest's and Hamilton's guns go into battery at the head of King and Queen Streets, firing down both into the storm.

events.title: Rall forms
events.text: The Rall regiment forms in King Street and marches up it toward the American guns; two Hessian 3-pounders get off six rounds each before half their crews are down and Weedon's Virginians charge and take them. The Lossberg regiment comes up Queen Street and is stopped by Forrest.

events.title: The orchard at Trenton
events.text: Rall rallies behind St Michael's church and leads his two regiments out of the streets into the orchard east of the town, then back in a counter-attack toward the American guns. Fire from the houses and the batteries breaks it; Rall is hit twice and carried into the church.

events.title: The Knyphausen regiment
events.text: Surrounded in the orchard, the Rall and Lossberg regiments ground their arms. The Knyphausen regiment tries to reach the creek above the bridge, bogs its guns in the mill-pond marsh, and is cut off by St Clair and Stark; it surrenders minutes after the rest. By ten it is over: 22 Hessians dead, about 900 prisoners, six guns, four Americans wounded.

events.title: Back to the river
events.text: Washington's council votes against pushing on. The army marches back nine miles through the storm with its prisoners and recrosses the Delaware that night.

events.title: The second crossing
events.text: On the 29th and 30th the army crosses again through heavy ice, two days' work, and camps south of the Assunpink at Trenton. On the last day of the year Washington offers ten dollars to any man who will stay six weeks past his enlistment; most of the Continentals step forward. Mifflin's and Cadwalader's militia march up from Bordentown and Crosswicks.

events.title: Cornwallis marches
events.text: Cornwallis leaves Princeton at dawn on 2 January with 5,500 men and 28 guns, Leslie's brigade dropped at Maidenhead. The roads are thawed to mud. Hand's riflemen, a thousand men with two guns, wait at Five Mile Run to slow him.

events.title: Hand's delaying action
events.text: Hand skirmishes at Five Mile Run, ambushes the van from the wooded bank of Shabakunk Creek and holds the British there searching the woods for half an hour, then stands again at Stockton Hollow. It costs Cornwallis the whole day.

events.title: Into Trenton
events.text: Hand's men fall back through the town firing from the houses; Hessian grenadiers come in with the bayonet. Washington sits his horse on the bridge while the rear guard files through under the guns on Mill Hill. The British reach the creek just before sunset.

events.title: The bridge
events.text: Three times the British come at the Assunpink: at the lower fords, then the Hessian grenadiers in column on the bridge, then the British in a solid column met with canister and a volley. 'The bridge looked red as blood.' Cornwallis calls it off at dark: 'we'll bag the fox in the morning'.

events.title: The council at the Douglass house
events.text: With the river at his back full of ice, Washington takes his officers' advice to slip away by the Quaker Bridge road and strike Princeton. The gun wheels are wrapped in rags; five hundred men stay to feed the fires and dig within the enemy's hearing.

events.title: The night march
events.text: The wind has gone north-west and the mud is frozen hard enough for the guns. From about one the army files east by Sandtown, through the scrub of the Barrens, over the Quaker Bridge and up the new-cut Sawmill road, twelve miles in the dark on ice.

events.title: Daylight at Stony Brook
events.text: At first light the column halts by the Quaker meeting house, two miles from Princeton and behind time. Mercer's brigade turns off along the brook to secure the Post Road bridge at Worth's Mill; Sullivan's division wheels right up the Sawmill road toward the town.

events.title: Mawhood turns back
events.text: Mawhood has marched the 17th and 55th for Maidenhead before dawn. From the hill beyond the bridge he sees Mercer's column in the sun and turns back over Stony Brook; both race for the orchard on William Clarke's rising ground.

events.title: The orchard
events.text: Mercer's men win the orchard and fire from its upper fence; the British volley goes high. Mawhood orders the bayonet. The line is overrun, both guns lost, Mercer's horse shot and Mercer clubbed and bayoneted by Joseph Clark's barn, Haslet shot through the head, Neil killed at his guns. Cadwalader's militia come up and break after a volley; Moulder's two 4-pounders hold on alone.

events.title: Washington's rally
events.text: Washington rides between the lines with Hitchcock's New Englanders, Hand's riflemen and the Virginians, halts them thirty yards from the British and gives the word. Hitchcock's volley and charge break Mawhood's line; the 17th cut their way out with the bayonet down the Post Road and over the bridge, chased by the Philadelphia Light Horse. 'It is a fine fox chase, my boys.'

events.title: Frog Hollow and Nassau Hall
events.text: Sullivan's division drives the 55th and the 40th from the ravine on Stockton's farm through Donop's earthwork and into the town. Two hundred flee north leaving two guns; Hamilton's battery puts a shot into Nassau Hall and 194 men inside surrender.

events.title: To Kingston
events.text: Washington gives up Brunswick for want of fresh troops and marches north-east as Leslie's advance guard appears at Stony Brook, where Kelly's party is tearing up the bridge. A straggler fires the 32-pounder from the earthwork and holds up Cornwallis for an hour. The British find Princeton empty at one.

events.title: After
events.text: Ten days: two posts taken, some 1,200 prisoners, Cornwallis's army drawn into the hills. The British give up all New Jersey but Brunswick and Amboy. Mercer dies at the Clarke house on 12 January. Washington goes into winter quarters at Morristown.

losses: Trenton: 4 wounded, 2 dead of cold on the march. Princeton: 25 to 44 killed, Mercer among them, and 40 wounded.
Trenton: 22 killed, 83 wounded, 896 captured. Princeton: by Howe's return 18 killed, 58 wounded and about 200 missing.
outcome.note: Washington claimed over 100 British killed and 300 taken at Princeton; the counts have never been reconciled.

sources: William S. Stryker, The Battles of Trenton and Princeton (1898): the Hessian quarters and picket posts, the regimental strengths and losses, the night march order, the Stony Brook bridge, Mawhood's sighting from the hill by Cochran's, the orchard fight, Nassau Hall and the 32-pounder.

Washington to Hancock, 27 December 1776 ('exactly at eight o'clock', 'three minutes after') and 5 January 1777; Knox's and Greene's letters; the Hessian court-martial testimony on Rall; Wiederhold's and Piel's diaries.
David Hackett Fischer, Washington's Crossing (2004): the storm 'about eleven', the orders of battle, the councils at the Douglass house, the freeze on the night of 2 January, Mawhood's brigade.

Richard M. Ketchum, The Winter Soldiers; the Trenton Historical Society's street plan and battle scripts (King Street is Warren, Queen Street is Broad); the Princeton Battlefield Society and the 2010 Milner Battle of Princeton Mapping Project for the Sawmill road and Maxwell's Field.
American Battlefield Trust (Trenton and Princeton); Washington Crossing Historic Park and State Park; the Old Barracks Museum.

Terrain: USGS 3DEP elevation at 73 m over a 22 km square. The Delaware and the creeks are traced from the grid, not surveyed; the 1776 roads follow their modern successors (Bear Tavern Road, Pennington Avenue, River Road, Route 206, Quaker Bridge and Mercer Roads).

What is reconstructed: the times inside the Trenton fight between 'exactly eight' and 'over by ten'; the hours of Hand's stands on 2 January; the start of the night march (sources say midnight to two); the hours at Princeton, anchored only by 'daylight', 'about eight' and 'two hours in the town'; brigade strengths on 3 January; and the places of the orchard, the Quaker Bridge and Cochran's hill, taken off the modern road net.
